en.title: Lanterns Premiere: Hal Jordan's Shocking Death Sparks DCU Debate
en.summary: HBO's gritty take on Green Lantern kicked off with a bang, leaving fans reeling from an unexpected hero's demise. The bold narrative choice ignites crucial conversations about the future of DC's cosmic storytelling.
en.body:
The wait is over for **HBO**'s ambitious foray into the cosmic side of the DC Universe with **Lanterns**. The series premiere has landed, and it's already making waves, not just with its grounded, noir-inspired aesthetic, but with a narrative gut-punch that has left many viewers and comic purists divided. From its opening moments, **Lanterns** signals that this is not your typical superhero fare, opting for a gritty, detective-driven approach that has drawn comparisons to *True Detective*.

The immediate fallout from the first episode centers on the fate of **Hal Jordan**, a character synonymous with the Green Lantern mantle. In a move that defied widespread expectations and seemingly ignored the hero's iconic status, Jordan is killed off within the premiere's closing moments, shot in the head. This decision, coupled with his limited use of the Green Lantern ring and minimal time in costume, has ignited a firestorm among fans, particularly those deeply invested in **Hal Jordan**'s journey. The showrunner, **Chris Mundy**, confirmed that the provocative hook originated from writer **Tom King**, known for his unconventional and often canon-bending interpretations of DC characters.

## A Bold Gamble for the DCU

This bold narrative choice by **Chris Mundy** and **Tom King** is precisely the kind of gamble the **DCU** needs to make. The Green Lantern franchise, with its inherently strange concept of intergalactic police force wielding imagination-powered rings, can easily become unwieldy or feel dated. By leaning into a darker, more grounded mystery, **Lanterns** aims to make these cosmic concepts accessible and compelling for a modern audience. The series' creators are clearly prioritizing a serialized, character-driven narrative over straightforward superheroics, a strategy that could redefine how audiences perceive these powerful beings.

> "Tom basically had the 30,000-foot view: ‘What if you did Green Lanterns True Detective-ish?’" — **Chris Mundy**

## Fan Reaction and the Future of Oa

The fan reaction has been swift and passionate. While many critics and a significant portion of the audience have praised the show's mature tone and innovative storytelling, a vocal segment of **Hal Jordan** loyalists feels betrayed. This division highlights the delicate balance showrunners must strike when adapting beloved characters for new mediums. The success of **Lanterns** hinges on its ability to retain its daring vision while still satisfying the core expectations of its fanbase. The series is poised to explore the wider **Green Lantern Corps**, including iconic locations like Oa and characters such as **Guy Gardner** and **Sinestro**, potentially weaving them into a larger cosmic tapestry that will connect with future **DCU** films and series.

## What's Next

With the first episode setting such a high bar for shock value and narrative ambition, the remaining seven episodes of **Lanterns** season one promise to be a thrilling exploration of the Green Lantern mythology. Future installments will undoubtedly delve deeper into the mystery surrounding **Hal Jordan**'s death and introduce a wider array of Lanterns and cosmic threats, all while building towards the eventual formation of a future Justice League. Details on a potential second season have not yet been announced.

content_raw: This article contains spoilers for Lanterns season 1 episode 1. The first episode of the HBO series Lanterns has received praise from almost everyone who watched it, from critics to casual fans to many comic book readers. But there’s one group of people who are not happy with the Green Lantern show, particularly what happens in the final moments. It’s not just that fans of Hal Jordan hated that the first episode ended with their hero dead from a bullet in his head. It’s that the series killed Hal after keeping him almost entirely out of costume, unmasked, and only making a few constructs with his ring. Those fans had a suspicion of whom to blame, a guy who had many times before taken DC Comics characters and reimagined them in wildly different ways in service of an unusual narrative. Those suspicions were confirmed this morning, when showrunner Chris Mundy told The Hollywood Reporter , that Tom King came up with the initial hook. “Tom basically had the 30,000-foot view: ‘What if you did Green Lanterns True Detective -ish?,'” he revealed. While some may hate the thought of turning intergalactic space cops into gritty sleuths, King’s unconventional, canon-defying approach may be exactly what the DCU needs to survive. As we’ve talked about a lot here at Den of Geek recently, Green Lantern is a weird franchise. It’s a series about people across the galaxy chosen to wield powerful rings that allow them to create whatever they can imagine. It’s a strange concept, and one that asks the reader to suspend disbelief. But for those who buy in, Green Lantern is one of the most compelling hero concepts in the DC Universe, one that lends itself to straightforward superhero action, or mind-bending, high-strangeness storytelling, as Al Ewing is demonstrating in the current Absolute Green Lantern series. Those who buy in are extremely passionate about the concept in the characters. So when Hal Jordan shows up in a panel of the 2018 miniseries Heroes in Crisis and admits, “I don’t even know what the hell ‘will’ is,” fans were furious. Furious, but unsurprised. Because Heroes in Crisis came from Tom King, a writer who has made his name with audacious stories that often treat canon and prior characterization as optional. His Batman run killed off Alfred, temporarily turned Nightwing into an amnesiac called Ric Grayson, and famously built to a marriage between Catwoman and Batman that never happened. In Strange Adventures , King turned Silver Age adventurer Adam Strange into a lying war criminal, forever hen-pecked by his Lady MacBeth-like wife. Heroes in Crisis may be the worst offender of all, in which the Flash Wally West gets so distraught about losing his family through the latest multiversal reboot that he kills a bunch of his friends, including fellow Teen Titan Arsenal (they got better).
